Distillation builds a new model from signals exposed by one or more teachers. The goal may be compression, lower latency, a deployable model family, or transfer of a behavior such as reasoning or tool use. The student does not inherit the teacher automatically; it learns only from the prompts, targets, and selection process it sees.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. distinguish logit, response, rationale, and trajectory distillation;
2. design teacher sampling and verification for a target student;
3. explain self-distillation, teacher ensembles, and long-to-short transfer;
4. separate capability transfer from style imitation; and
5. evaluate a model family under quality, latency, memory, and token budgets.

## Distilling distributions

[Knowledge distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531) [@hinton2015distillation] trains a student against softened teacher probabilities. For logits $z_i$ and temperature $T$,

$$
q_i(T)=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j/T)}.
$$

Higher temperature reveals relative probability assigned to alternatives. Logit access provides a dense target at every token but is usually unavailable for closed teachers and expensive to retain for large vocabularies.

## Distilling sequences and explanations

When only text is available, the teacher can produce final answers, rationales, critiques, tool trajectories, or preference pairs. [Distilling step-by-step](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.02301) [@hsieh2023distilling] studies rationales as additional supervision for smaller models. The important control is answer-only data under the same prompt and token budget: otherwise more explanatory text is confounded with more training signal.

A robust pipeline can sample several teacher outputs, verify objective components, rank the survivors, deduplicate strategies, and retain failures for contrastive or critique data. Teacher confidence is not a substitute for an independent checker.

## Self-distillation and model families

In self-distillation, a model or earlier checkpoint generates targets for another version of the same family. This can standardize behavior and exploit additional sampling compute, but it can also narrow diversity and preserve systematic errors.

A model family introduces a routing decision: which checkpoint should answer which request? Evaluate each size at matched conditions and construct a Pareto frontier over quality, latency, memory, energy, and generated tokens. The smallest checkpoint is not cheapest if it needs many retries or an excessively long trace.

## Long-to-short reasoning transfer

Reasoning teachers may use long exploratory traces while students are expected to answer compactly. Long-to-short transfer can train on selected traces, compressed rationales, verified subgoals, or final answers. Each target makes a different claim:

| Target | What the student can learn | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| final answer | input–output mapping | no visible method |
| full rationale | teacher procedure and style | verbosity and invalid steps |
| compressed rationale | selected intermediate structure | lossy or judge-biased compression |
| verified steps | locally checked transitions | expensive, incomplete coverage |

## Studio: one teacher, four targets

Construct four equal-token datasets from one teacher: answer only, full rationale, compressed rationale, and verified steps. Train the same student initialization with the same update budget. Evaluate in-distribution and harder held-out tasks, then report accuracy, calibration, output length, latency, and failure types.

The deliverable includes the teacher prompt distribution, sampling settings, verifier, target-construction code, and a family-level Pareto plot containing the base student, distilled students, and teacher.

## What to remember

1. Distillation transfers the signal the teacher exposes, not the whole teacher.
2. Prompt coverage and target construction determine which behavior can transfer.
3. Rationales add both information and confounding tokens; controls must match budget.
4. Self-distillation can amplify a family's strengths and its blind spots.
5. A useful model family is evaluated as a quality–cost frontier.
